exam_name: ISTQB Certified Tester Test Automation Engineering

questions.domain: Introduction and Objectives for Test Automation
questions.question: A team automates 100% of its UI regression cases but build feedback still takes 3 hours and half the failures are environment issues. Which objective was missed?

options.A: Coverage; they should automate more cases
options.B: Efficiency and reliability: automation value depends on fast, trustworthy feedback, not just raw case count
options.C: Documentation; they need more test plans
options.D: Nothing; the automation is successful

questions.explanation: High coverage with slow, unreliable execution does not deliver the intended benefits. Objectives include quick feedback and low false-failure rates, which need attention here.

questions.domain: Introduction and Objectives for Test Automation
questions.question: Which test is generally the WEAKEST automation candidate?

options.A: A stable login regression run every build
options.B: A one-time data-migration check for a feature being decommissioned next month
options.C: An API contract test run in CI
options.D: A boundary-value test on a core calculation

questions.explanation: Automation pays off with repetition and longevity. A single-use check on a soon-to-be-removed feature will not recover its automation cost.

questions.domain: Introduction and Objectives for Test Automation
questions.question: A stakeholder expects automation to "cut the test team in half." What is the most accurate response?

options.A: Agree; that is the purpose of automation
options.B: Automation shifts effort rather than simply removing it: testers move to test design, exploratory testing, framework maintenance, and analysis of results
options.C: Automation always increases headcount needs
options.D: Refuse to introduce automation

questions.explanation: Automation reallocates human effort toward higher-value activities and adds maintenance work; it rarely translates directly into large headcount cuts.

questions.domain: Introduction and Objectives for Test Automation
questions.question: The SUT is a legacy desktop app with no automation-friendly APIs and dynamically generated control IDs. Which realistic approach best manages the risk?

options.A: Automate everything through the UI with recorded scripts
options.B: Prioritise adding testability (stable identifiers, a thin automation API), automate the most valuable stable flows, and keep exploratory/manual testing for the rest
options.C: Abandon testing the app
options.D: Wait until the app is rewritten before any testing

questions.explanation: When testability is poor, the pragmatic path is to improve it where feasible, automate selectively on stable high-value flows, and rely on manual testing elsewhere.

questions.question: Two tools pass the technical fit check. Which additional evaluation dimension most affects long-term total cost of ownership?

options.A: The tool's splash-screen animation
options.B: Maintainability of the tests it produces, reporting/CI integration, required skills, and community or vendor support
options.C: The number of menu items
options.D: Whether the tool has a dark theme

questions.explanation: Beyond "can it drive the SUT," TCO is dominated by how maintainable the resulting tests are, how well it integrates and reports, and the skills and support available.

questions.question: A pilot automation project should be scoped to:

options.A: The entire regression suite so results are conclusive
options.B: A representative but small slice that exercises the SUT's key interfaces and the intended framework patterns, with clear success criteria
options.C: Only the simplest possible test so it always passes
options.D: A feature nobody uses

questions.explanation: A useful pilot is small yet representative: it stresses the real interfaces and patterns and is judged against predefined criteria before scaling up.

questions.question: Which is the strongest argument for automating at the API layer rather than the UI where possible?

options.A: API tests look nicer in reports
options.B: API tests are typically faster, more stable, and less affected by cosmetic UI change, giving better ROI for logic and integration coverage
options.C: UI tests cannot be automated at all
options.D: API tests need no maintenance ever

questions.explanation: Testing below the UI avoids rendering flakiness and layout churn, runs faster, and pinpoints failures closer to the cause, so business logic is best covered there.

questions.question: A team wants automation but the SUT team randomises DOM IDs each deploy. The best collaboration ask is:

options.A: Ask developers to add stable, semantic test identifiers (for example data-testid) to key elements
options.B: Ask developers to stop deploying
options.C: Ask for a slower release cadence
options.D: Ask for the source code to be obfuscated

questions.explanation: Stable, purpose-built test hooks are a low-cost testability improvement that removes a major source of UI-test fragility.

questions.question: Placing SUT-interface details only in the adaptation layer of the gTAA primarily achieves:

options.A: Faster test execution
options.B: Isolation of change: when an interface changes, only the adapters need updating, not every test case
options.C: Elimination of the need for test data
options.D: Automatic test generation

questions.explanation: Confining interface coupling to adapters means interface changes have a small, localised maintenance footprint.

questions.question: A framework mixes locators, waits, business steps, and assertions directly in each test method. Which refactor gives the biggest maintainability improvement first?

options.A: Rename the test methods
options.B: Introduce a page/screen object (or service) layer so UI/interface details are encapsulated and reused
options.C: Add more comments
options.D: Increase the timeout values

questions.explanation: Encapsulating interface interactions behind page/service objects removes duplication and localises UI changes, the highest-leverage structural fix.

questions.question: Keyword-driven testing is most beneficial when:

options.A: Only one person will ever write tests and they are all throwaway
options.B: Non-technical stakeholders need to read or author tests, and many tests reuse the same business actions
options.C: There are no repeated actions across tests
options.D: The SUT has no user interface or API

questions.explanation: Keyword-driven frameworks shine when business-level reuse is high and less-technical people participate in test creation or review.

questions.question: In data-driven testing, which is the correct handling of an input row that is expected to be rejected by the SUT?

options.A: Skip it, negative cases cannot be data-driven
options.B: Include an expected-result field per row so the same script asserts success or the correct error/validation for each input
options.C: Put it in a separate framework
options.D: Mark the whole suite as failed

questions.explanation: Each data row should carry its expected outcome (including expected validation errors) so one parametrised script handles positive and negative cases.

questions.question: A BDD scenario reads: "When I do lots of stuff, Then everything works." What is the main problem?

options.A: It uses Given/When/Then
options.B: The steps are vague and non-verifiable; BDD scenarios must express concrete behaviour with checkable outcomes
options.C: It is written in English
options.D: It has only two steps

questions.explanation: BDD's value is precise, example-based behaviour. Vague steps cannot be reliably automated or reviewed and defeat the purpose of shared understanding.

questions.question: Which describes an appropriate use of the test generation layer of the gTAA?

options.A: Storing screenshots of failures
options.B: Deriving test cases or test data automatically, for example from models, requirements, or combinatorial techniques
options.C: Rendering the HTML report
options.D: Connecting to the SUT database

questions.explanation: The generation layer produces tests/data (model-based, combinatorial, requirement-derived), separate from defining, executing, or adapting them.

questions.question: A team shares one automation framework across web, mobile, and API tests. Which design choice best supports this?

options.A: Hard-code the web driver everywhere
options.B: Define tests against business-level abstractions, with pluggable adapters per interface behind a common interface
options.C: Duplicate all test logic three times
options.D: Only support whichever interface was built first

questions.explanation: A common abstraction with interchangeable adapters lets the same high-level tests (or shared steps) run against different interfaces without rewriting logic.

questions.question: A UI test intermittently fails at "click Submit" because the button is sometimes not yet enabled. The correct fix is to:

options.A: Add a fixed 5-second sleep before every click
options.B: Wait explicitly for the button to be present, visible, and enabled before clicking
options.C: Retry the whole test 10 times
options.D: Delete the assertion

questions.explanation: Condition-based explicit waits synchronise the test with the application state, removing the race without the wasted time and fragility of fixed sleeps.

questions.question: Blanket automatic retry of every failed test is risky mainly because it:

options.A: Makes reports shorter
options.B: Can mask genuine intermittent product defects and hides the true flakiness rate
options.C: Speeds up the suite
options.D: Improves locator stability

questions.explanation: Retries turn some real intermittent bugs green and remove visibility of flakiness. Retry should be limited, logged, and paired with flaky-test tracking and fixing.

questions.question: Tests pass locally but fail in CI. Which is the most likely systemic cause to investigate first?

options.A: The tester's keyboard layout
options.B: Environment differences: browser/driver versions, headless mode, screen size, timing under load, data state, or missing services
options.C: The colour of the CI logo
options.D: The number of commits that day

questions.explanation: Local-vs-CI divergence almost always comes from environment/config/timing/data differences; aligning environments and controlling state resolves most of it.

questions.question: A regression suite has grown to 6 hours and blocks the pipeline. Which contingency is most aligned with good practice?

options.A: Delete random tests until it is fast
options.B: Tier the suite (fast checks on every commit, fuller regression nightly), parallelise execution, and remove redundant or low-value tests based on risk
options.C: Run the suite only once per release
options.D: Disable assertions to speed it up

questions.explanation: Managing suite growth means layering by feedback need, parallelising, and pruning by value/risk, not arbitrary deletion or disabling checks.

questions.question: Which practice most improves the reliability of tests that depend on external third-party services?

options.A: Always calling the real service in every run
options.B: Using service virtualisation / stubs for most tests, with a small set of real-integration tests run separately
options.C: Removing all tests that touch external services
options.D: Ignoring failures from those tests

questions.explanation: Virtualising unstable or rate-limited dependencies makes the bulk of tests deterministic; a focused real-integration subset still verifies the actual connection.

questions.question: A key automation engineer leaves and no one else understands the framework. This is an example of which risk, and the best mitigation?

options.A: Tooling risk; buy a new tool
options.B: Knowledge/bus-factor risk; mitigate with documentation, coding standards, pairing, code review, and shared ownership
options.C: Data risk; refresh the test data
options.D: Schedule risk; add more testers to unrelated tasks

questions.explanation: Single-person knowledge is a deployment risk for the TAS. Documentation, standards, reviews, and collective ownership spread understanding.

questions.question: A report shows 98% pass rate, but 200 of the 1,000 tests were skipped. What is the reporting problem?

options.A: None; skipped tests do not matter
options.B: The headline pass rate is misleading unless skipped/blocked counts and reasons are shown prominently alongside it
options.C: The report is too detailed
options.D: 98% is too low to report

questions.explanation: A pass rate computed over only executed tests hides gaps. Skipped, blocked, and not-run figures must be visible so stakeholders see true coverage of the run.

questions.question: Which metric best helps decide where to invest in reducing automation maintenance cost?

options.A: Total number of test files
options.B: Failures per test over time and change frequency of the areas they cover, to find brittle high-churn tests
options.C: Average length of test names
options.D: Number of testers who like the framework

questions.explanation: Tracking which tests fail often and cover frequently-changing code identifies the maintenance hotspots worth refactoring or re-targeting.

questions.question: "Defect detection effectiveness" of the automated suite is best approximated by:

options.A: The number of tests that exist
options.B: The proportion of defects the automated suite catches before release versus those found later (in later phases or production)
options.C: The suite's execution time
options.D: The number of assertions per test

questions.explanation: Effectiveness is about outcomes: how many real defects the suite catches early relative to those that escape it, often expressed via defect detection percentage.

questions.question: A manager wants a single "automation health" dashboard. Which combination is most informative?

options.A: Only the latest pass/fail count
options.B: Pass rate trend, flaky-test rate, mean execution time, coverage against risk areas, and open test-maintenance debt
options.C: Only the number of new tests added this week
options.D: Only lines of test code

questions.explanation: Health is multi-dimensional: outcome trend, stability, speed, risk coverage, and backlog of maintenance work together show whether the suite is trustworthy and sustainable.

questions.question: Which is a valid caution about using "code coverage of the SUT achieved by automated tests" as a target?

options.A: It is impossible to measure
options.B: High code coverage does not imply strong assertions or good scenario coverage; tests can execute code without meaningfully verifying behaviour
options.C: It always correlates perfectly with quality
options.D: It only applies to manual testing

questions.explanation: Coverage shows what was executed, not what was checked. Weak or missing assertions can leave defects undetected despite high coverage numbers.

questions.domain: Transitioning Manual Testing to an Automated Environment
questions.question: A team plans to automate its 800 manual regression cases "as-is." Which risk should be raised?

options.A: Automating verbatim may carry over redundancy, unclear steps, and low-value cases; the set should be triaged and redesigned for automation first
options.B: There is no risk; a 1:1 conversion is always optimal
options.C: Manual cases can never be automated
options.D: The cases will run too fast

questions.explanation: A blind conversion inherits bloat and ambiguity. Triaging by value/risk and rewriting for determinism yields a leaner, more maintainable suite.

questions.domain: Transitioning Manual Testing to an Automated Environment
questions.question: During transition, which is the best way to keep confidence while automation coverage is still partial?

options.A: Stop all manual testing immediately
options.B: Run a blended approach: automated checks for covered areas plus targeted manual/exploratory testing for the rest, tracking coverage explicitly
options.C: Release without any regression testing
options.D: Automate only after 100% of cases are converted

questions.explanation: A phased, blended model maintains regression confidence: automation where it exists, human testing for the gaps, with visibility of what each covers.

questions.domain: Transitioning Manual Testing to an Automated Environment
questions.question: A manual case says "verify the report looks correct." To automate it, the tester should:

options.A: Automate a screenshot and never check it
options.B: Decompose "looks correct" into specific verifiable checks (values, totals, presence/order of sections, formatting rules), automating those and leaving genuine visual judgement to a human or visual-diff tool
options.C: Skip the case entirely
options.D: Assert the report file size only

questions.explanation: Vague expectations must be turned into concrete assertions. Aspects that truly need visual judgement can use visual regression tooling or stay manual.

questions.domain: Transitioning Manual Testing to an Automated Environment
questions.question: Which is a realistic expectation for the first two or three sprints of a new automation initiative?

options.A: Net reduction in total testing effort
options.B: Net increase in effort as the framework, environment, and first tests are built, with payback in later cycles
options.C: Zero defects escaping to production
options.D: Complete replacement of the test team

questions.explanation: Early sprints are investment-heavy. Leaders should plan for and communicate the delayed return so the initiative is not judged prematurely.

questions.question: A test passes even after the feature it checks is completely removed from the SUT. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: The SUT is working perfectly
options.B: The assertion is weak or absent (for example it only checks the page loads), so it cannot detect the missing behaviour
options.C: The test runs too quickly
options.D: The report tool is broken

questions.explanation: A test that stays green when its target behaviour is gone has no real verification. It needs meaningful assertions and a check that it fails when the behaviour is broken.

questions.question: Which review activity is most specific to verifying test automation code quality?

options.A: Checking that locators are robust, waits are condition-based, assertions are meaningful, and tests are independent and idempotent
options.B: Checking the SUT's marketing copy
options.C: Checking the office seating plan
options.D: Checking the CI server's disk temperature

questions.explanation: Automation-specific review focuses on locator strategy, synchronisation, assertion strength, isolation, and repeatability, the properties that make tests trustworthy.

questions.question: How can a team verify that their automation framework's reporting is trustworthy?

options.A: Assume it is correct because the vendor built it
options.B: Deliberately introduce known passing and failing conditions and confirm the report classifies and evidences each correctly
options.C: Only check the report once a year
options.D: Compare the report font to the brand guide

questions.explanation: Seeding known outcomes and confirming the report reflects them (with correct status and evidence) validates the reporting chain, including screenshots and logs.

questions.question: A new adapter is added to the TAS. Which verification step is most important before relying on it?

options.A: Confirm it compiles
options.B: Run a set of tests through the adapter whose outcomes are known, including negative cases, and confirm correct pass/fail behaviour and error reporting
options.C: Rename its methods for consistency
options.D: Add it to the documentation index

questions.explanation: The adapter is a critical component; it must be exercised against known-good and known-bad conditions to prove it drives and observes the interface correctly.

questions.question: In a CI pipeline, where should long end-to-end UI tests usually sit?

options.A: As a blocking gate on every commit
options.B: In a later stage or nightly run, after fast unit/API/smoke stages, so quick feedback is not delayed
options.C: They should not be in CI at all
options.D: Before the code is even written

questions.explanation: A staged pipeline runs cheap, fast tests first for rapid feedback and reserves slower, broader E2E suites for later stages or scheduled runs.

questions.question: The "test pyramid" guidance suggests that a healthy automated suite has:

options.A: Mostly slow end-to-end UI tests and few unit tests
options.B: Many fast unit tests, fewer service/API tests, and relatively few end-to-end UI tests
options.C: Equal numbers at every level
options.D: Only manual tests

questions.explanation: The pyramid favours a large base of fast, isolated tests and a small tip of expensive end-to-end tests, optimising speed, stability, and diagnosis.

questions.question: Consumer-driven contract testing reduces the need for large end-to-end environments because it:

options.A: Tests the UI pixel by pixel
options.B: Verifies each service pair's interface expectations independently, catching incompatibilities without deploying the whole system together
options.C: Removes the need for any integration testing
options.D: Only checks database schemas

questions.explanation: Contract tests assert compatibility at each boundary in isolation, so many integration risks are caught cheaply and full-stack environments are needed less often.

questions.question: A retrospective finds the automated suite is distrusted because "it fails all the time for no reason." Which continuous-improvement action addresses the root issue?

options.A: Hide the failing tests from the report
options.B: Quarantine flaky tests, fix or rewrite them with a tracked backlog, and enforce a policy that a red suite blocks merges once trusted
options.C: Stop running the suite
options.D: Add many more tests to dilute the failures

questions.explanation: Restoring trust means isolating and fixing flakiness systematically, then treating suite results as authoritative. Hiding failures or adding noise makes it worse.

questions.question: Which is a sound reason to periodically DELETE automated tests?

options.A: To reduce the line count for its own sake
options.B: They are duplicated by better tests, cover removed features, or provide no additional risk coverage while adding maintenance and runtime cost
options.C: Any test that has ever failed
options.D: Tests written by people who left the team

questions.explanation: Pruning redundant, obsolete, or zero-value tests keeps the suite fast and maintainable; the criterion is coverage value versus cost, not blame or raw size.

questions.question: A team stores test data as literals scattered through hundreds of test methods. The best improvement is to:

options.A: Add comments next to each literal
options.B: Centralise test data in managed fixtures/builders or external sources, with clear ownership and per-environment variants
options.C: Copy the literals into a spreadsheet and keep them in the code too
options.D: Randomise all values at runtime

questions.explanation: Managed, centralised test data (fixtures, builders, or data files) removes duplication, eases updates, and supports different environments.

questions.question: Which is the most robust strategy for test data in an automated regression suite?

options.A: Depend on whatever data happens to be in the shared environment
options.B: Have each test create and clean up the data it needs (via API or fixtures), or use isolated, reset-to-baseline data per run
options.C: Never delete any test data
options.D: Use production data directly with real customer PII

questions.explanation: Deterministic tests own their data lifecycle or run against a controlled baseline, avoiding failures from shared-state drift and avoiding PII exposure.

questions.domain: Introduction and Objectives for Test Automation
questions.question: Under a Scrum process, when is automation of a story's acceptance checks ideally done?

options.A: Several releases after the story ships
options.B: Within the same iteration as the story, so the checks protect the feature immediately and "done" includes automated coverage
options.C: Only during a dedicated automation-only sprint months later
options.D: Never in agile teams

questions.explanation: In-sprint automation keeps regression protection current and supports a definition of done that includes automated verification, avoiding a growing automation backlog.

questions.question: A proof-of-concept shows a tool can drive the SUT, but the resulting scripts are unreadable and each takes hours to stabilise. What should the evaluation conclude?

options.A: The tool is fully suitable; proceed to scale
options.B: Technical feasibility is necessary but not sufficient; maintainability and stabilisation cost are failing criteria and must be weighed before adopting
options.C: Ignore maintainability; only feasibility matters
options.D: Adopt it and hire more people to maintain scripts

questions.explanation: A PoC must judge maintainability and effort-to-stabilise, not just "can it click." Poor results here are a legitimate reason to reject or mitigate.

questions.question: Which statement about combining BDD with the Page Object Model is correct?

options.A: They are incompatible
options.B: Gherkin steps can call page/screen objects, keeping scenarios business-readable while UI details stay encapsulated and reusable
options.C: BDD replaces the need for any code layers
options.D: Page objects must contain the Gherkin text

questions.explanation: A common, effective layering: features in Gherkin, step definitions orchestrate, page/screen objects handle interface interaction.

questions.question: A stakeholder asks "how much manual regression effort has automation saved this quarter?" Which is the most defensible answer approach?

options.A: Guess a large number
options.B: Estimate from automated executions x historical manual time per case, minus automation build/maintenance effort, and present it as a range with assumptions
options.C: Say it cannot be estimated at all
options.D: Report only the number of tests written

questions.explanation: A credible ROI figure nets saved manual execution time against automation investment and is presented transparently as an estimate with stated assumptions.

questions.question: Which situation indicates a "false positive" (a test that misses a real defect)?

options.A: A test fails because a locator changed but the feature works
options.B: A payment feature has a rounding bug, yet the automated payment tests all pass because they only check that a confirmation page appears
options.C: A test is skipped due to a tag filter
options.D: A test times out waiting for a slow environment

questions.explanation: The tests pass while a genuine defect exists because their assertions are too shallow, this is a missed-defect (false positive) situation, not a false alarm.

questions.question: "Shift-left" for test automation most directly means:

options.A: Running tests only after release
options.B: Involving automation earlier, unit and API tests written alongside code, so defects are found closer to their introduction
options.C: Moving the CI server to another data centre
options.D: Left-aligning the test report

questions.explanation: Shift-left brings testing and automation into earlier stages of development, where feedback is faster and fixes are cheaper.

questions.question: A cross-browser suite fails only on one browser due to a real rendering difference in the SUT. How should this be handled in the automation strategy?

options.A: Suppress the browser from the suite so it stays green
options.B: Keep the coverage, log a product defect, and only add a documented conditional expectation if the difference is an accepted, known limitation
options.C: Delete all cross-browser tests
options.D: Change the assertion to accept any result

questions.explanation: A genuine SUT difference is a finding, not a test problem. It is raised as a defect; conditional handling is only appropriate for consciously accepted differences.

questions.domain: Transitioning Manual Testing to an Automated Environment
questions.question: Which skill gap most often blocks a manual-heavy team from succeeding with automation, and how is it best addressed?

options.A: Typing speed; buy faster keyboards
options.B: Programming and framework-design skills; address with training, pairing with developers, hiring, and starting with a well-structured framework and standards
options.C: Knowledge of the office layout; provide a map
options.D: Ability to write test plans; stop writing them

questions.explanation: Sustainable automation needs coding and design capability. Training, pairing, targeted hiring, and a solid framework/standards close the gap.

questions.question: Which is the best reason to keep assertions out of page objects and in the tests (or step definitions)?

options.A: Page objects cannot contain code
options.B: It keeps page objects focused on interaction and reusable across tests with different expectations, while intent/verification stays visible in the test
options.C: Assertions slow down page objects
options.D: It is required by every language

questions.explanation: Separating "how to interact" (page object) from "what we expect" (test) maximises reuse and keeps each test's purpose explicit; some minimal state checks in page objects are still acceptable.

questions.question: Which reporting practice best supports fast triage of CI failures across a large team?

options.A: A plain text file with only pass/fail counts
options.B: Per-failure evidence (screenshot, DOM/log snapshot, request/response, stack trace), grouping of failures by likely cause, and a link to the exact build and commit
options.C: Emailing the full console output to everyone
options.D: Only storing the final exit code

questions.explanation: Rich, grouped, traceable failure evidence lets engineers quickly distinguish product defects, environment issues, and flakiness and route them correctly.

questions.domain: Introduction and Objectives for Test Automation
questions.question: Which statement about automation and exploratory testing is correct?

options.A: Automation makes exploratory testing obsolete
options.B: They are complementary: automation handles repeatable regression checks, freeing testers to do more exploratory testing for new risks
options.C: Exploratory testing must be fully scripted before automation
options.D: Only one of them can be used per project

questions.explanation: Automation and exploratory testing address different needs. Automating the repetitive checks creates time and headspace for valuable exploratory work.

questions.question: A pull request adds 20 tests that all pass. Which review question most protects test quality?

options.A: Do the test names sound nice?
options.B: For each test, if the behaviour it targets were broken, would this test fail? (Are the assertions specific and sufficient?)
options.C: Are there exactly 20 tests?
options.D: Were they written on a Friday?

questions.explanation: The core question for new tests is whether they have real detection power, meaningful, targeted assertions that would fail on the relevant defect.

questions.question: Which is a good use of tags/labels on automated tests in a CI/CD context?

options.A: To make the code file longer
options.B: To select subsets for different pipeline stages (smoke, regression, slow, area-owned) and to route failures to owners
options.C: To hide tests from execution permanently
options.D: To store the tester's name only

questions.explanation: Tagging enables flexible suite selection per stage and ownership-based triage without maintaining separate test lists.

questions.question: A newly added AI-based visual-testing tool flags dozens of "differences" every run due to minor anti-aliasing changes. What is the pragmatic response?

options.A: Disable visual testing entirely
options.B: Tune the comparison sensitivity/ignore regions, baseline intentionally, and route only meaningful visual changes for human review
options.C: Accept every diff automatically
options.D: Fail the whole build on any pixel change forever

questions.explanation: Visual diffing needs calibration: sensitivity thresholds, ignore regions for volatile areas, deliberate baselining, and human review of genuine changes, otherwise noise destroys its value.
